about.features:
- Three analyses: single plot, multiple plots (spatial) and temporal (one plot over the years).
- Reads `.xlsx`, `.csv` and `.txt`, normalises column names and finds the table and the plot area.
- Species resolved from an editable regional species table (names, codes and genus abbreviations).
- Density, basal area, mean DBH, mean and canopy height, stems per tree and mortality.
- Relative density, dominance and frequency, and the importance value (IVI).
- DBH classes with configurable cutoffs and the Holdridge complexity index.
- A data-check panel, publication-quality figures and PDF, Excel, CSV and TXT exports (including the table of every chart), heights in metres or centimetres and results with two decimals.

- Holdridge, L.R. (1967). *Life zone ecology*. Tropical Science Center, San José.
- Pool, D.J., Snedaker, S.C. & Lugo, A.E. (1977). Structure of mangrove forests in Florida, Puerto Rico, Mexico, and Costa Rica. *Biotropica* 9(3): 195-212.
- Estrada, G.C.D., Soares, M.L.G., Chaves, F.O. & Cavalcanti, V.F. (2013). Analysis of the structural variability of mangrove forests through the physiographic types approach. *Aquatic Botany* 111: 135-143. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aquabot.2013.06.003
- Soares, M.L.G. et al. (2017). Mangrove forests associated with salt flats: a case study from southeast Brazil. *Brazilian Journal of Oceanography* 65(2): 102-115.

about.title: About MangueTREE
about.what: MangueTREE is an open-source Python engine with a Streamlit interface for the structural and phytosociological analysis of mangrove forest plots. It reads field inventories (one row per stem), checks the data, and computes the parameters used in mangrove structure studies.

colon.chart.reference_note: Reference (Jiménez, Lugo and Cintrón 1985): as a stand develops, stem density falls from more than 500,000 propagules per hectare to about 2,000 stems per hectare, with a mean DBH of 2.5 cm, in less than five years. Colonization reaches 40-70 seedlings per m² in Rhizophora and 140-330 per m² in Avicennia. The curve in the paper (Fig. 2) is schematic and has no equation.
colon.chart.regression_equation: {label}ln(density) = {a} + {b} × ln(age), that is, density = {c} × age^{b}, with standard error of b of {se}, r² = {r2} and n = {n}.
colon.chart.regression_need: Give the start year of at least one plot, with at least three points of positive age and two different age values.
colon.chart.regression_note: Least squares fit on log-log scale, using only positive density and age. The points are repeated measures of the same plots, so n counts points and not independent plots, and the standard error and r² are descriptive.
colon.chart.schema_note: Schematic redrawn from Figure 2 of Jiménez, Lugo and Cintrón (1985), which shows the normal changes of stem density of a mangrove stand without catastrophic disturbance. The paper gives no equation or values for this curve, so the drawing is only qualitative. On the right, the observed density of juveniles in your plots, to compare the shape of the curves.
colon.chart.schema_title: Schematic of stand development (schematic, not to scale)
colon.chart.start_hint: Year in which the plot was established (0 = not given). The values come from Figure 2.2 of Estevam (2019) and can be edited. Age is the collection year minus that year, using only ages above zero, and counts the time since the plot was set up, not since colonization really began: individuals of an earlier cohort ("<1998") already existed when the first plots were set up.

home.computes:
- **Structure:** density (stems/ha), basal area (m²/ha), mean DBH, mean and canopy height, stems per tree, mortality (stems and basal area).
- **Phytosociology:** relative density, dominance and frequency, and the **importance value (IVI)**; Cintrón & Schaeffer-Novelli (1984).
- **DBH classes:** distribution by diameter class (configurable cutoffs).
- **Holdridge complexity index**, computed for DBH > 2.5 cm and DBH > 10 cm; Pool, Snedaker & Lugo (1977).
- **Spatial comparison** between plots and **temporal analysis** of one plot over the years.
- **Export** of tables (Excel/CSV) and **PDF reports**.
home.description: MangueTREE turns field inventories of mangrove plots into structural and phytosociological parameters, DBH class distributions and comparisons between plots and over the years. Upload a spreadsheet, review the data-check panel and export the tables and figures.
home.examples: Two example files from the Guaratiba mangrove (Rio de Janeiro, Brazil) are in the `data/` folder of the [repository]({repo}): `guaratiba_T2_2009.xlsx` (three plots, one sheet per plot; for Single plot and Multiple plots) and `guaratiba_H2_2003_2025.xlsx` (plot H2 surveyed 15 times; for Temporal).

map.no_coordinates: The file has no coordinate columns (latitude and longitude), so there is no map to show.
method.dbh_classes: Default DBH classes: below 2.5 cm, 2.5 to below 10 cm, and 10 cm or more; the cutoffs can be changed in the sidebar (Cintrón & Schaeffer-Novelli 1984, p. 92). A stem of exactly 2.5 cm falls in the middle class and one of exactly 10 cm in the upper class.
method.heights_live_only: Mean height, its standard deviation and canopy height use live stems only: the field protocol used at NEMA/UERJ does not record height on dead trees (Estrada et al. 2013).
method.holdridge: CI = s · d · b · h · 10⁻³, where s = number of species, d = number of stems, b = basal area (m²) and h = stand height (m), all per 0.1 ha; Holdridge (1967), as applied to mangroves by Pool et al. (1977). In each index, s, d and b use only live stems with DBH above the cutoff. Adaptation: h is the mean of the 10 tallest live-stem heights in the plot (Pool et al. 1977 used the tallest tree of each subplot).
method.ivi_multi: **How the IVI is calculated.** IVI = RDe + RDo + RF, the sum of three relative values (Cintrón & Schaeffer-Novelli 1984, p. 96). **RDe** (relative density) = live stems of the species ÷ all live stems × 100. **RDo** (relative dominance) = basal area of the species ÷ total live basal area × 100. **RF** (relative frequency) = frequency of the species ÷ sum of the frequencies of all species × 100, the frequency being the % of plots in which the species occurs. Here the plots are the sampling units, and density and basal area pool the stems over the summed plot areas. Height is not part of the IVI.
method.ivi_needs_units: The IVI needs more than one sampling unit, because frequency depends on them (Cintrón & Schaeffer-Novelli 1984, p. 96). For a single plot the table shows relative density and relative dominance. The IVI is on the Multiple plots page.
method.mean_dbh: Mean DBH is the diameter of the tree of mean basal area (the quadratic mean), not the arithmetic mean of the DBH values (Cintrón & Schaeffer-Novelli 1984).
method.q_note: The De Liocourt quotient q is descriptive; its interpretation depends on the stand context.
multi.intro: **Spatial** comparison between plots. Upload an Excel file with **one sheet per plot**: the app computes the parameters of each plot, compares them and builds the importance value index (IVI) treating the plots as sampling units.

multi.radar_note: Radar chart: each axis is a structural parameter and each polygon is a plot. Normalised values: normalised value = plot value ÷ highest value of that parameter among the plots. So the plot with the highest value sits at 1 and the others show their fraction of that maximum. The chart compares the shape of each plot's profile, not absolute values (those are in the table below).

multi.species_note: Each column adds up, in each plot, the density (stems per hectare) or basal area (m² per hectare) of each species, separating live (L) and dead (D) stems. Density = stems ÷ plot area; basal area = sum of π/4 × DBH² of each stem (Cintrón & Schaeffer-Novelli 1984). The 100% option divides each column by the plot total.
temporal.series_note: Each point is the value of the plot in that year, calculated as in the single-plot analysis: density = live stems ÷ plot area; basal area = sum of π/4 × DBH² of the stems; mean DBH = diameter of the tree of mean basal area (Cintrón & Schaeffer-Novelli 1984); canopy height = mean of the 10 tallest live stems (NEMA/UERJ protocol, Estrada et al. 2013).
single.note.composition: Share of each species in the live basal area of the plot: species basal area ÷ total live basal area × 100, where the basal area of a stem is π/4 × DBH² (Cintrón & Schaeffer-Novelli 1984).
single.note.classes: Class density = live stems of the class ÷ plot area (stems/ha); class basal area = sum of π/4 × DBH² of the stems of the class ÷ plot area (m²/ha). Classes are closed on the left: [lower limit, upper limit) (Cintrón & Schaeffer-Novelli 1984).
single.note.hist: Histogram of the DBH of the live stems of the plot (25 bins), stacked by species; the height of each column is the number of stems.
single.note.height_dbh: Each point is a live stem with measured DBH and height. For each species, the dashed line is the least-squares linear regression, height = a × DBH + b, with its R² (equation and R² in the table beside it). Dead stems and stems without DBH or height are left out.
single.note.profile: Vertical profile of the live stems with height and DBH. Circles: each stem at its height, in increasing order, sized by DBH. Stems: each stem as a stalk up to its height. Strata: number of stems per height class (chosen width), stacked by species. Distribution by species: violin of the heights of each species.
temporal.sd_hint: The standard deviation exists for mean height (of the stems measured); the other parameters are shown without error bars.
